paragraphs: We saw in the last chapter what causes the various kinds or forms of government to be distinguished according to the number of their members. It remains in this chapter to discover how the division is made.

First, the Sovereign may place the government in the hands of the whole people, or of most of them, so that there are more citizens who are magistrates than citizens who are mere private individuals. This form of government is called _democracy_.
Or the Sovereign may restrict the government to a small number, so that there are more private citizens than magistrates. This is called _aristocracy_.

Finally, the Sovereign may gather the whole government into the hands of a single magistrate, from whom all the others derive their power. This third form is the most common, and is called _monarchy_, or royal government.

Note that all these forms, or at least the first two, come in degrees, and can differ very widely. For democracy may include the whole people, or may be restricted to half. Aristocracy, in its turn, may be narrowed continuously from half the people down to the smallest possible number. Even royalty can be shared to some degree. Sparta always had two kings, as its constitution provided; and the Roman Empire saw as many as eight emperors at once, and no one could say the Empire was divided. Thus there is a point at which each form of government shades into the next, and it becomes clear that, under three general names, government can really take as many different forms as the State has citizens.

There are even more. For the government may also, in certain respects, be subdivided into other parts, one administered in one way and one in another. The combination of the three forms may then produce a multitude of mixed forms, each of which can be multiplied by all the simple forms.
There has always been much dispute about the best form of government, without anyone considering that each is the best in some cases and the worst in others.

If the number of supreme magistrates in each State should stand in inverse ratio to the number of citizens, it follows that, in general, democratic government suits small States, aristocratic government suits middle-sized ones, and monarchy suits great ones. This rule follows directly from the principle laid down. But the countless circumstances that may produce exceptions cannot be counted.
